prompt: Before the upload, a ping through the new 5 Mbit/s link took 0.106 ms. Why did shaping the link change nothing?

choices.text: Pings are too small for tc to shape
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it: the same ping took 221 ms a minute later.

choices.text: The queue was empty, so nothing waited
choices.why: Right. A slow link only delays packets that arrive while others are waiting to leave.

choices.text: tc rules take effect only after a restart
choices.why: They apply at once; tc qdisc show listed the queue straight away.

choices.text: ICMP goes around the queueing discipline
choices.why: Every packet leaving eth1 goes through its qdisc, pings included.

prompt: A full queue holds 100 packets of 1514 bytes. How many milliseconds does it take to drain at 5 Mbit/s?
hint: Bytes to bits, then divide by 5,000,000.

prompt: Why does one upload keep the queue in front of the slow link full, rather than full now and then?

choices.text: iperf3 sends at a fixed rate above 5 Mbit/s
choices.why: A TCP test has no fixed rate; it goes as fast as the path allows.

choices.text: The upload's packets are marked with a higher priority
choices.why: They were unmarked, and with one queue a mark would change nothing.

choices.text: TCP speeds up until a packet is lost, then climbs again
choices.why: Right. It finds the limit by filling the queue until it overflows: 163 retransmissions in five seconds.

choices.text: The link slows down when it gets busy
choices.why: The link sends at 5 Mbit/s, busy or not; what grows is the line in front of it.

prompt: An office's calls break up only while somebody sends a large file. What is the calls' actual problem?
hint: Where does a voice packet spend its time?

choices.text: They wait behind the file in the uplink's queue
choices.why: Right. A call needs little bandwidth and a short wait, and the file takes the wait away.

choices.text: The line has run out of capacity for voice
choices.why: A call is a small fraction of 5 Mbit/s; it is short of turns, not of bandwidth.

choices.text: The file's packets damage the voice packets
choices.why: Packets in a queue do not touch each other; they only wait.

choices.text: The router's processor is overloaded by the transfer
choices.why: Five megabits is nothing for a router's CPU; the queue explains every number measured.

prompt: EF is DSCP 46. What is the whole ToS byte, in decimal, that tcpdump prints as 0xb8?
hint: Six bits moved two places to the left.

prompt: A capture shows tos 0x88. Which DSCP does the packet carry?

choices.text: 136, the byte itself
choices.why: 136 is the whole byte, ECN bits included; the DSCP is its top six bits.

choices.text: 34, which is AF41
choices.why: Right. 136 divided by 4 is 34, the class for interactive video.

choices.text: 88, read straight off the capture
choices.why: 0x88 is hexadecimal; as decimal it is 136, and the DSCP is a quarter of that.

choices.text: 46, since every marked packet is EF
choices.why: EF is 0xb8. Other classes have other codes.

prompt: With one queue, the EF-marked ping averaged 20 ms and the unmarked one 65 ms. What does that show about the mark?
hint: Look at the unmarked run's slowest reply.

choices.text: It cut the delay by two thirds
choices.why: Take out the one 221 ms reply and the other four averaged 26 ms, the same as the marked run's.

choices.text: Nothing: one slow reply lifted the average
choices.why: Right. Both runs waited in the same queue; only the timing of one reply differed.

choices.text: It helped on the routers that honour EF
choices.why: No router on this path had a class for EF at that point.

choices.text: EF packets are smaller, so they drain faster
choices.why: The mark changes one byte's value, not the packet's size: both pings were 84 bytes.

prompt: A router with a single queue sends packets in the order they ___, whatever their DSCP says.
Match each piece of the tc setup to the job it does.

pairs.right: Decides which class a packet is in

prompt: tc -s showed class 1:10 with 5 packets and 490 bytes. What were they?

choices.text: Five upload packets that happened to be marked EF on the way
choices.why: An upload packet is about 1500 bytes; five of them would be about 7,500.

choices.text: HTB's own control messages
choices.why: HTB sends nothing of its own; it only orders what others send.

choices.text: Five packets the class dropped
choices.why: Its counter says dropped 0; these were sent.

choices.text: The five marked pings, 98 bytes each with Ethernet
choices.why: Right. 84 bytes of IP and 14 of Ethernet header, five times.

prompt: Everybody in the office starts marking all their traffic EF. With this lesson's HTB, how much can class 1:20 still count on?
hint: rate is a guarantee; prio decides who gets what is spare.

choices.text: Nothing, since EF is served first
choices.why: That would be strict priority. HTB gives every class its rate before prio decides anything.

choices.text: 4 Mbit/s, its guaranteed rate
choices.why: Right. The flood gets its 1 Mbit/s and whatever 1:20 leaves unused, no more.

choices.text: 1 Mbit/s, what is left after voice
choices.why: That swaps the two rates: voice is guaranteed 1, the rest 4.

choices.text: The whole 5 Mbit/s, because EF stops at 1 Mbit/s
choices.why: EF's ceil is 5mbit: it may borrow whatever 1:20 is not using.

prompt: What does the mask 0xfc in `match ip dsfield 0xb8 0xfc` do?

choices.text: Rewrites the byte to 0xfc
choices.why: A filter reads; it writes nothing into the packet.

choices.text: Matches any DSCP at or above EF
choices.why: A mask selects bits to compare; it is not a range.

choices.text: Compares the six DSCP bits and ignores ECN
choices.why: Right. A packet marked EF matches whatever its two ECN bits say.

choices.text: Sets how many packets the class may queue
choices.why: That is pfifo limit 100.

prompt: After the two nftables rules, the laptop's EF-marked ping averaged 26 ms again. Why?

choices.text: hq rewrote its mark to cs0 as it arrived
choices.why: Right. The laptop still marks EF; hq no longer believes it.

choices.text: The laptop stopped marking once the rule existed
choices.why: Nothing told the laptop; the same ping -Q 0xb8 ran.

choices.text: The voice class was full of files' traffic
choices.why: files sent a single six-byte datagram, and later.

choices.text: The ISP reset the byte on the way
choices.why: The delay is added at hq's queue, before the ISP sees anything.

prompt: Where does a trust boundary belong?

choices.text: On the ISP's router
choices.why: By then the packets have crossed your whole network on marks nobody checked.

choices.text: In each laptop's network settings
choices.why: The laptop is the party that cannot be trusted to mark itself.

choices.text: On the first device the network's owner controls
choices.why: Right. Usually the access switch, or hq in this lab.

choices.text: On the server that receives the traffic
choices.why: The queues that matter are passed before the server sees anything.

prompt: The two nftables rules are swapped: first the one marking files' UDP 5004 as EF, then `ip dscp set cs0` for everything from eth0. What does files' datagram leave with?
hint: Setting a field is not a verdict.

choices.text: EF, because the first matching rule wins
choices.why: That is true of accept and drop. A set statement changes the packet and evaluation carries on.

choices.text: cs0, because the later rule overwrites the EF
choices.why: Right. Both rules run; the last one to write the byte decides it.

choices.text: Nothing, because it is dropped
choices.why: Neither rule drops anything; the chain's policy is accept.

choices.text: Whatever files wrote into it
choices.why: Both rules overwrite the byte, so files' own mark is gone either way.

prompt: The ISP's router printed tos 0xb8 on every marked packet. What did it do with the mark?

choices.text: Put the packets in its priority queue
choices.why: It has no classes configured, so there is no such queue.

choices.text: Reset it to zero at the edge of its network
choices.why: The captures show 0xb8 intact on the ISP's side.

choices.text: Nothing, it forwarded them like any other
choices.why: Right. A mark means what each router is configured to make of it.

choices.text: Dropped the packets that had no mark
choices.why: Unmarked traffic, the upload included, went through.

prompt: Large downloads at the office make calls break up as well. Why can hq's classes on eth1 not fix that on their own?
hint: Which way does eth1's queue face?

choices.text: Downloads are marked cs0 by the provider
choices.why: The mark on a download does not matter here; hq's classes shape what leaves, not what arrives.

choices.text: The queue that fills is at the provider's end
choices.why: Right. The download waits before it reaches hq, in a queue hq cannot configure.

choices.text: HTB classes work on UDP only
choices.why: The upload in this lesson was TCP and was classified like anything else.

choices.text: tc cannot count packets that are coming in
choices.why: Counting is not the problem; the waiting happens before they arrive.

prompt: Put in order what happens at hq to files' voice datagram, from the LAN to the ISP.
items: The nftables chain sets its DSCP to EF
The u32 filter puts it in class 1:10
HTB sends it before class 1:20's queue
trap: The mark is written at prerouting, before routing, and read by the classifier on the way out of eth1.

prompt: Which of these would shorten the wait of a call on hq's uplink during an upload? Choose all that apply.
hint: Keep the voice out of the long line, or make the line short.

choices.text: A voice class, selected by DSCP and sent first
choices.why: Right: 0.065 ms in this lesson.

choices.text: Marking the calls EF with a single queue
choices.why: Measured: the marked ping waited 26 ms like everything else.

choices.text: A queue manager such as fq_codel that keeps the queue short
choices.why: Right: a shorter line is a shorter wait for everybody, calls included.

choices.text: A longer queue of 1000 packets
choices.why: A longer queue that stays full is a longer wait: that is bufferbloat.

prompt: A manager's laptop is given EF on all its traffic, to make it faster. What happens to the office's calls while it uploads?
hint: Which queue does the upload now share?

choices.text: Nothing changes; the laptop just gets faster
choices.why: The upload now sits in the voice class, and so do the calls.

choices.text: They wait behind the upload in the voice class
choices.why: Right. Priority only helps a class that stays small; this one no longer does.

choices.text: The laptop's upload is dropped as out of profile
choices.why: Nothing in this setup drops for being EF; 1:10 may borrow up to 5 Mbit/s.

choices.text: The calls are moved to class 1:20
choices.why: The filter still sends EF to 1:10; the calls are exactly where they were.

prompt: A queue that stays full and adds delay to every packet behind it is called ___.
